title: Given an array of n plus 1 integers where each integer is between 1 and n inclusive, exactly one number is repeated. Find the duplicate without modifying the array and using only constant extra space. (LeetCode: Find the Duplicate Number)
shortTitle: Find the Duplicate Number (Cycle Detection on Array Indices)

s1_definition.profdef: Finding the single duplicate in an array of n plus 1 values ranging from 1 to n uses Floyd's cycle detection by treating each value as a pointer to the next index. Because values lie in the valid index range and one value repeats, following value-as-index links forms a linked structure with a cycle, and the cycle's entry node is the duplicate. This runs in linear time with constant extra space and does not modify the array.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh has a list of n plus 1 locker numbers, each between 1 and n, and exactly one locker number appears twice. He treats each slot's value as an instruction to jump to that index next, like following a treasure map where each spot tells you where to go. Because one number repeats, two different slots eventually point to the same place, which creates a loop in the jump path. The spot where the loop begins is exactly the duplicated locker number.
s1_definition.oneliner: Treat each value as a next-index pointer; the duplicate is the entry of the cycle those pointers form.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Finding the single duplicate in an array of n plus 1 values ranging from 1 to n uses Floyd's cycle detection by treating each value as a pointer to the next index. Because values lie in the valid index range and one value repeats, following value-as-index links forms a linked structure with a cycle, and the cycle's entry node is the duplicate. This runs in linear time with constant extra space and does not modify the array.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh has a list of n plus 1 locker numbers, each between 1 and n, and exactly one locker number appears twice. He treats each slot's value as an instruction to jump to that index next, like following a treasure map where each spot tells you where to go. Because one number repeats, two different slots eventually point to the same place, which creates a loop in the jump path. The spot where the loop begins is exactly the duplicated locker number.

**One line to remember:** Treat each value as a next-index pointer; the duplicate is the entry of the cycle those pointers form.

sections.s2_technical:
The clever insight is to view the array as a function from index to index: from position i you jump to position arr[i]. Since every value is between 1 and n and there are n plus 1 positions, this jumping sequence must eventually revisit a position, forming a cycle. Crucially, because exactly one value is duplicated, two different positions point into the same position, and that shared target is the entry of the cycle, which corresponds to the duplicate value.

So we apply Floyd's tortoise and hare on these jumps. Phase one: slow jumps one step, meaning slow becomes arr[slow], and fast jumps two steps, meaning fast becomes arr[arr[fast]], until they meet inside the cycle. Phase two: we reset one pointer to the start index, then advance both one jump at a time, and the index where they meet is the duplicate number.

A finance usage example: suppose locker numbers are `[1, 3, 4, 2, 2]`. Starting both pointers at index 0, slow jumps to arr[0] which is 1, then arr[1] which is 3, then arr[3] which is 2, and so on, while fast jumps twice as fast. They meet inside the cycle. Resetting one pointer to index 0 and advancing both one jump at a time, they converge at the value 2, which is the duplicate.

The senior-level nuance: this approach does not modify the array and uses constant space, satisfying the strict constraints. Alternatives include sorting, which modifies the array, or a hash set, which uses linear extra space, or binary search on the value range using a counting argument, which is also constant space but n-log-n time. The cycle-detection method is linear time and constant space, the strongest combination, and it relies on the guarantee that values are in the range 1 to n so that no value points outside the array. The reason the duplicate is the cycle entry is the same pointer-convergence argument as the linked list cycle start problem.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India assigns locker reference numbers from a fixed range to a batch of safe-deposit lockers, and a provisioning bug occasionally issues one reference number twice while all others are unique. The audit tool must find the single duplicated reference quickly, without modifying the original list, because the list is used immutably elsewhere, and without allocating large extra memory, because the batches can be huge.

Problem 2 — The constraints forbid sorting, which would reorder the immutable list, and forbid a hash set, which would use memory proportional to the batch size, so the tool uses the cycle-detection trick that treats each reference value as a jump index.

The code defines a `DuplicateRefFinder` class with a `findDuplicate` method implementing Floyd's two-phase algorithm over value-as-index jumps. A runnable demo seeds a locker reference list with one duplicate and logs the duplicated reference.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the locker references `[1, 3, 4, 2, 2]`, where exactly one value is duplicated.

Step 1: Phase one begins. Both slow and fast start at the value at index 0, which is 1. In the first iteration slow jumps to the value at index 1, which is 3, and fast jumps twice: to index 1 giving 3, then to index 3 giving 2, so fast is 2.

Step 2: Next iteration, slow jumps to the value at index 3, which is 2, and fast jumps twice again from its current position. The pointers continue chasing through the implied links.

Step 3: Because the value 2 is duplicated, the jump path forms a cycle, and the slow and fast pointers eventually land on the same value inside that cycle, ending phase one.

Step 4: Phase two begins. A new pointer is set to the value at index 0, which is 1, while slow stays at the meeting value. Both now advance one jump at a time.

Step 5: The two pointers converge at the value 2, which is the entry of the cycle and therefore the duplicated reference. The method logs a warning naming the duplicate and returns 2. The original array was never modified.

Final output:

```
Oct 27, 2026 7:00:00 PM com.bank.locker.DuplicateRefDemo main
INFO: Locker references: [1, 3, 4, 2, 2]
WARNING: Duplicate locker reference = 2
INFO: The duplicated reference is 2
```


sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the single duplicate in an array of n plus one values, each between one and n, under the strict constraints of not modifying the array and using only constant extra space, is solved beautifully by reinterpreting the array as a set of pointers. I treat each value as an instruction to jump to that index next, so from position i I go to position arr at i. Because every value is a valid index and one value repeats, following these jumps must form a cycle, and the entry point of that cycle is exactly the duplicated value.

That turns the problem into Floyd's cycle detection. In the first phase I run a slow pointer that takes one jump per step and a fast pointer that takes two jumps per step until they meet inside the cycle. In the second phase I reset one pointer to the starting value and then advance both pointers one jump at a time, and the value where they converge is the duplicate. This is the same convergence argument as finding the start of a linked list cycle, just applied to array indices instead of list nodes.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in a locker audit tool. We assigned locker reference numbers from a fixed range, and a provisioning bug occasionally issued one reference twice while all others were unique. The audit tool had to find the single duplicate quickly without modifying the original list, because that list was used immutably elsewhere, and without allocating memory proportional to the batch size, because batches were huge. The value-as-index cycle detection met both constraints exactly.

The senior-level point I make is why this method wins over the alternatives given the constraints. Sorting would find the duplicate but reorders the array, which is forbidden. A hash set would work in linear time but uses linear extra space, also forbidden. A binary search over the value range using a counting argument respects the constraints but costs n-log-n time. The cycle-detection approach is the only one that is simultaneously linear time, constant space, and non-destructive, and it depends on the guarantee that values lie in the valid index range so that no jump ever leaves the array. Explaining that this guarantee is what makes the pointer interpretation valid is what demonstrates I understand why the trick works rather than just memorizing it.
